Ecological efficiency is hardly ever above 10% because most of the energy that comes into a trophic level never ends up as new body mass at the next one. Nitrogen starts as N2 gas in the air...Nitrogen-fixing bacteria (like Rhizobium in root nodules, and cyanobacteria in the water) fix N2 into ammonia, NH3, which picks up a proton in the soil and becomes ammonium, NH4+. Then nitrifying bacteria do nitrification in two steps: Nitrosomonas turns NH4+ into nitrite, NO2-, and Nitrobacter turns nitrite into nitrate, NO3-. Nitrate is the form most plants take up through their roots. Inside the root the plant reduces the nitrate back down to NH4+ using nitrate reductase, and then the NH4+ gets attached to a carbon skeleton to build amino acids like glutamate. Those amino acids get moved up to the leaf and joined together by ribosomes into a protein.

The trigger is climate, not crowding, so the effect isn't a function of density. Density-dependent factors get stronger as N rises; the drought would've hit just as hard at low N. (i) Food competition, density-dependent: the seed supply on Daphne Major is basically fixed per year. Divide that fixed supply by more and more birds and each individual gets less. At 300 birds there's plenty of the small easy seeds to go around; at 1,200 birds the small seeds get stripped fast and a lot of finches are stuck trying to crack big Tribulus seeds that only the biggest-beaked birds can handle. So starvation goes up and reproductive success goes down, and how bad it gets scales directly with how many birds there are - that's the definition of density-dependent. (ii) Disease transmission, density-dependent: pathogens spread by contact, so the more crowded the birds are the more contacts happen per bird per day. At high density they're packed onto the same seed patches and roosts, so an infected finch passes it to many others before it dies, and the disease can take off. At low density the same pathogen may burn out because the sick bird never runs into enough susceptible birds. Step 1 - Nitrogen fixation. Atmospheric N2 gas is very stable (triple bond) and plants can't use it. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria, like Rhizobium living in legume root nodules or free-living Azotobacter and cyanobacteria, use the enzyme nitrogenase to convert N2 into ammonia, NH3, which picks up a proton in the soil water to become ammonium, NH4+.
Step 2 - Nitrification. This happens in two stages, both done by chemoautotrophic soil bacteria. Nitrosomonas oxidizes NH4+ into nitrite, NO2-. Then Nitrobacter oxidizes the nitrite into nitrate, NO3-.
Step 3 - Assimilation/uptake. Nitrate is very soluble so the plant's root hairs take NO3- up out of the soil solution. Inside the plant, enzymes (nitrate reductase and then nitrite reductase) reduce the NO3- back down to NH4+.
Step 4 - Amino acid synthesis. The plant attaches that ammonium to a carbon skeleton from the Krebs cycle (like alpha-ketoglutarate) to build glutamate and then the other amino acids by transamination. Those amino acids get shipped to the leaf cell, where a ribosome links them by peptide bonds using the mRNA copied from a gene, and now the nitrogen atom is sitting in the backbone of a leaf protein like rubisco.

Why tropical rainforest GPP beats boreal even per square meter:
- Light: rainforests sit near the equator so sunlight hits close to perpendicular all year and daylength barely changes. Boreal forests are at high latitude, so light comes in at a low angle and winter days are very short. More photons absorbed means more photosynthesis.
- Temperature: rainforests stay around 25-27 C year round, near optimum for rubisco and the Calvin cycle enzymes. Boreal forests are below freezing for months, so photosynthesis basically shuts off for a big chunk of the year. Rainforest has a 12 month growing season, taiga has maybe 3-4 months.
- Water: rainforests get 2000+ mm of rain spread through the year, so stomata can stay open without the plant dehydrating and CO2 keeps flowing in. In boreal winter the water is frozen and therefore physiologically unavailable, which is basically a drought.
- Nutrient cycling: it's hot and humid so decomposers work extremely fast and nutrients get released and reabsorbed by roots and mycorrhizae almost immediately. In the taiga, cold slows decomposition and acidic conifer needles build up as litter, so nitrogen and phosphorus stay locked in undecomposed organic matter and limit growth.

Hypothesis: If sharks are removed from a coral reef, then reef species diversity will decrease over 5 years, because the sharks are keystone predators that keep mid-level predators like groupers from overexploiting smaller fish and grazers. Measurements: I'd pick several reefs where shark fishing has removed the sharks and several similar reefs inside a marine protected area where sharks are still present, as controls. Every year for 5 years I would run standardized belt transects (say 50 m x 5 m, same depth, same season, same divers or same video method) and record every fish species seen and how many of each. From those counts I'd get species richness and also a Shannon or Simpson diversity index so evenness counts too, not just number of species. I'd also record percent live coral cover and algae cover since those drive habitat structure. Determination: Compare the change in the diversity index over the 5 years in the shark-removed reefs vs the control reefs. If the removal reefs drop significantly (a t-test or ANOVA on the index, p<0.05) while the controls stay flat, that supports the prediction. If both groups change the same way, that points at something else. Limitation: The reefs aren't randomly assigned, they're wherever sharks already happen to be missing, so the shark-free reefs may already differ (more fishing pressure overall, closer to shore, more runoff). That confounds fishing with shark loss. Also 5 years may be shorter than the time it takes slow-growing corals and long-lived fish to respond, so a real effect could be missed.
